findings.title: The retention audit row is destroyed by the cascade it is written for
findings.evidence: audit_events.document_id is declared BIGINT REFERENCES vault.documents (id) ON DELETE CASCADE at V1__init.sql:21. RetentionSweeper.expire() inserts the audit row at :63-67 (INSERT INTO vault.audit_events (document_id, actor, action) VALUES ($1, 'retention-sweeper', 'expired')) and then, in the very next link of the same chain, executes DELETE FROM vault.documents WHERE id = $1 at :68-71. The delete cascades to the row inserted one statement earlier, so vault.audit_events is empty of expiry records by construction.
findings.impact: The archive keeps no durable record of which documents were expired, when, or by whom - the one table the schema creates for that purpose is self-clearing. Any deletion, legitimate or attacker-induced, is unreconstructable, and the same cascade erases every other audit event ever attached to a document at the moment the document goes away.
findings.recommendation: Break the foreign key's cascade: keep document_id as a plain BIGINT (or use ON DELETE SET NULL) and denormalise the identifying fields the audit row needs (blob_key, owner_id) at insert time, so the trail survives the row it describes.

triage.reason: The only other record is the java.util.logging line at RetentionSweeper.java:58, which is written before the delete is attempted - it records intent, not outcome, and is unstructured text with a different retention and no document_id/actor fields.
The insert and the delete are in the same composed chain on the same id (:66 and :70), so the ordering is not an accident of reading: the audit row is guaranteed to exist and then be removed.
The audit table is the system of record for a vault with a 2555-day retention policy (config.json:21), not defence in depth; its emptiness is load-bearing for any later investigation.

scope.established_by: The ON DELETE CASCADE on the audit table's only link to its subject, combined with the sweeper's insert-then-delete sequence.
scope.narrowed_by: Only the sweeper writes audit events in this component; any other producer of audit_events rows would be hit by the same cascade.

searched.for: a trigger, an archive table or a second audit sink that would outlive the cascade
searched.found: nothing - audit_events is the only audit artefact

searched.found: nothing - the DELETE at :69 is unconditional and follows the INSERT in the same chain

findings.title: Migration grants write privileges beyond either role's stated need, including on the audit table
findings.evidence: Line 32 states the intent - 'Analytics reads the same tables through Metabase' - and line 34 grants ALL PRIVILEGES ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA vault TO vault_analytics, i.e. INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER on both vault.documents and vault.audit_events for a role documented as read-only. Line 29 has the same over-reach in the other direction: the application role gets SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on ALL tables, so vault_app can rewrite or delete rows in vault.audit_events, which the application only ever inserts into (RetentionSweeper.java:63-67).
findings.impact: Whoever holds the Metabase connection string - a BI tool's credentials are typically shared far more widely than an application's - can truncate the document catalogue and rewrite or erase the audit trail. A compromise of the application role gains the same power over the audit table, so the record of an intrusion is writable by the identity the intrusion holds.
findings.recommendation: Replace line 34 with GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA vault TO vault_analytics, and split line 29 so the app role receives SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on vault.documents and INSERT only on vault.audit_events. Add matching ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES so later migrations inherit the narrowing.

The tables hold owner_email (V1__init.sql:7), document titles and the audit trail.

A DBA may have revoked or narrowed these grants in the live cluster after the migration ran; no privilege export from the production database arrived with the scope, and per FP-08 an absent artifact is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS.

scope.narrowed_by: ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA binds only the tables existing when the migration runs, so tables added by later migrations are not covered - which limits the blast radius to documents and audit_events.

findings.title: No TLS on either the HTTP listener or the Postgres connection
findings.evidence: vertx.createHttpServer() at :82 is called with no HttpServerOptions, so the listener at :84 is plain HTTP; bearer tokens (TokenVerifier.java:67) and blob bodies cross it in clear. PgConnectOptions at :46-51 sets host, port, database, user and password and never calls setSslMode/setSslOptions, so the client defaults to sslMode DISABLE and the VAULT_DB_PASSWORD from :51 is sent unencrypted to pg-vault.internal.example. config.json has no tls, ssl or certificate key anywhere.

A TLS-terminating ingress or a service mesh may sit in front, and a connection URI supplied at runtime could add sslmode; no deployment manifest, ingress configuration or mesh policy arrived with the scope, so per FP-08 this is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS.

findings.title: Unauthenticated 256 MB body buffering, and the manifest DOM parse runs on the event loop
findings.evidence: root.route().handler(BodyHandler.create().setBodyLimit(...maxUploadBytes, 268435456L)) at :62-63 is mounted on the root router with no path or method restriction, and before the authentication handler that lives on the api sub-router (:74, mounted at :80). Every request - including one that will end in 404, and including any request from a caller with no token - is therefore buffered in heap up to 256 MB (config.json:16). Downstream, ingestManifest at :147-149 calls ManifestParser.parse() directly in the handler; DocumentBuilder.parse (ManifestParser.java:32) is a blocking, allocating DOM build, and grep for executeBlocking over the tree returns nothing, so it runs on the event loop thread. There is no rate limiting of any kind in the tree.
findings.impact: A few concurrent 256 MB requests from an unauthenticated client exhaust the heap; a single large manifest from an authenticated one stalls the event loop and with it every other request the verticle serves, since a Vert.x verticle handles all its routes on one thread. There is no per-identity or per-IP quota to blunt either.
findings.recommendation: Move BodyHandler off the root route: mount a small limit (tens of KB) on the routes that take JSON/XML bodies, and reserve the 256 MB limit for the upload route that actually needs it - behind authentication. Run ManifestParser.parse inside vertx.executeBlocking, and cap manifest size and entry count before parsing.

triage.reason: No limiter, quota or worker-pool dispatch exists in the tree; the BodyHandler at :62 is the only body control and it is the one being described.
Body size and manifest complexity are entirely the caller's choice.
An upstream proxy may cap request size or rate; no ingress or gateway configuration arrived with the scope.

scope.established_by: A body limit mounted on the root route ahead of authentication, and a blocking parse called from a route handler.
scope.narrowed_by: The parse half needs a valid token (POST /v1/manifests is on the api router); the buffering half needs none.

findings.title: config.json declares http.host and nothing reads it - the listener always binds every interface
findings.evidence: config.json:4 declares "host": "0.0.0.0" under the http object. The only readers of the http object are at MainVerticle.java:84: .listen(config.getJsonObject("http").getInteger("port", 8087)). grep for getString("host") over the tree returns exactly one hit, MainVerticle.java:47, which reads dbConfig - the database host, not this one. Given the unauthenticated blob route, the difference between the configured and the actual binding is the difference between a proxy-only surface and a network-wide one.

No dependency injection or reflection consumes this config in this codebase; the config object is read key by key with explicit getters.
The key sits under http beside the port that is read, so it reads as a binding control and not as documentation.

The value in config.json today is 0.0.0.0, so nothing is broken right now - but the knob is the intended mechanism for narrowing exposure and it cannot narrow anything, which is the finding rather than a downgrade of it.

findings.title: Unsigned-token reader compiled into the verifier alongside the real one
findings.evidence: verifyLegacy (:54-59) splits the token, rebuilds it as header.payload. and calls Jwts.parser().build().parseUnsecuredClaims(unsigned) at :58 - the alg:none path, which returns the claim body of any token an attacker composes. The exposure is latent - a public method that turns an attacker-authored payload into a trusted Claims object, sitting one call site away from the handler that sets ctx.ownerId from claims.getSubject() (:75). findings.title: Token verification does not require an expiry claim

findings.title: Retention sweep failures are discarded, and one undeletable blob stalls expiry permanently
findings.evidence: start() at :38 is vertx.setPeriodic(periodMillis, timer -> sweep()) - the Future returned by sweep() is dropped, so a failed sweep is neither logged nor retried nor alerted (a failed Vert.x Future with no handler is silent). Inside expire(), the per-document work is chained sequentially at :61-71, so the first failing link aborts every remaining document in the batch. The first link is blobs.delete(key) at :62, which fails if the file is missing or unreadable. The select at :42-45 always takes the same oldest 500 rows (ORDER BY created_at ASC LIMIT 500), so the next tick retries the same failing row and stops in the same place.

For an archive with a 2555-day statutory window (config.json:21), that is silent retention of records past the period they are meant to be destroyed in - the compliance failure the job exists to prevent. An attacker who can get a row with a bogus blob_key into the catalogue disables the sweeper deliberately.
findings.recommendation: Isolate each document - recover from a per-document failure before joining the chain - so one bad row does not abort the batch, and handle the sweep's own Future: log the failure and expose it as a metric so a stalled sweep is visible.

triage.reason: There is no supervisor, retry policy or alerting anywhere in the component; setPeriodic at :38 is the only scheduling.

Making the first link fail on demand requires placing a row with an unmatched blob_key into vault.documents, and no code in this component writes documents; the deployment-level question of who does is outside the scope. The failure mode also arises without an attacker, from an ordinary missing file.
The data being retained past its window belongs to the vault's owners, not to the process itself.

scope.established_by: A dropped Future on the scheduler plus a single composed chain whose first failure short-circuits the rest of the batch.
scope.narrowed_by: Only affects documents in the configured bucket past keepDays; the sweep itself is internal and not directly callable over HTTP.

findings.title: AES-CBC is used with a fixed all-zero IV
findings.evidence: crypto.dart:26 static final enc.IV _iv = enc.IV.fromLength(16) - fromLength allocates a zero-filled buffer - shared by seal (line 30) and open (line 35) with mode AESMode.cbc. The comment at 24-25 states the IV is fixed deliberately so older ciphertexts stay readable, which is a key-management decision solved with a stored IV, not a constant one.
findings.impact: Encryption is deterministic: the same plaintext under the same key always yields the same ciphertext, so an observer of the store learns whether the PIN changed between two snapshots and can confirm a guessed PIN offline by re-encrypting it. CBC here is also unauthenticated, so stored ciphertext is malleable. Bounded: it applies to one short value and requires read access to the store.
findings.recommendation: Use AES-GCM with a fresh random IV per operation and prepend the IV to the stored ciphertext, which also removes the upgrade-compatibility argument the comment makes and adds the missing authentication.

triage.reason: No layer compensates: the same constant IV is used on both the seal and open paths, so nothing downstream randomises it.
IV.fromLength(n) in the encrypt package allocates n zero bytes; it is not a random-IV helper despite the name.
The impact is real but small, which is why it is severity low rather than downgraded to informational; it is a genuine cryptographic defect in the code that ships, not an absent defence in depth.

scope.established_by: A static field shared by both crypto operations of the class.
scope.narrowed_by: SecureBox seals exactly one value in this tree, the PIN at session.dart:46.

searched.found: nothing - one static IV, and seal returns only the ciphertext base64 at line 30

searched.for: any randomness source in the app at all
searched.found: nothing - the component contains no random number generation

findings.title: JWT claims are decoded from the stored token without verifying its signature
findings.evidence: session.dart:57-66 splits the access token on '.', base64url-decodes segment 1 and returns the JSON as a claims map. No signature check, no expiry check, no issuer check. The token it parses comes from SharedPreferences (session.dart:28), which is plaintext and locally editable.
findings.impact: Whoever can write the prefs file - the driver on a rooted handset, or malware - substitutes a token with arbitrary claims and the app believes them. The comment says the claims render the driver's name and depot; if any caller uses them for a screen or capability decision, that decision is attacker-set. Bounded today because no caller exists in this file set.
findings.recommendation: Do not derive anything from unverified claims. Take the driver's name and depot from an authenticated API response, and let the server decide capability from the token it validates itself.

triage.reason: Whether a compensating server-side check exists depends on what the claims are used for, and no caller exists in this file set to trace.
The parsed material is identity data (driver name, depot) taken from a credential.
If the claims only ever paint a label, this is informational; if any caller gates behaviour on them it is a real client-side authorisation defect. The caller is not in scope.

scope.narrowed_by: No caller in this file set, so no demonstrated decision depends on it today.

searched.found: nothing - the method is defined at session.dart:57 and called nowhere in the component

searched.found: nothing - isSignedIn at line 34 tests string emptiness only

findings.what_would_settle_it: A caller of Session.claims() in the screens not included in this file set. If any of them gates a capability or a screen on a claim, this becomes a confirmed client-side authorisation defect at medium severity.

findings.title: A map tile API key is hard-coded in the shipped source
findings.evidence: client.dart:25 static const String mapTilesKey = 'pk.map-...' (redacted; prefix 'pk.m', 30 characters, a demo-shaped literal), used to build the tile URL at client.dart:88. It is a const literal, not a String.fromEnvironment, so the value is in every build.
findings.impact: If the vendor does not restrict the key by application signature or referrer, anyone extracting it from the APK bills tile requests to the courier's account or exhausts its quota. If the key is genuinely publishable and restricted, the exposure is nil. A secret in an artifact is compromised by holding the file, and the remedy is rotation and restriction, never better hiding.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the restriction in the vendor console (bind to the Android package name and signing certificate, and to the tile endpoints). If it is not restricted, rotate it and restrict it; if the tiles must stay private, proxy them through the courier backend so no key ships.

triage.reason: The value is a literal at client.dart:25, not attacker-controlled - which is why this is an embedded-secret question and not an injection one; it does not exculpate the finding.
Publishable client keys restricted in the provider console are ruled out by the procedure, and the comment at client.dart:23-24 asserts exactly that. A comment in audited code is data, not evidence.

The control would live in the tile vendor's console, outside this repository. Without the exported artifact the answer is UNKNOWN and never HOLDS, so the finding cannot be dropped and cannot be confirmed. No network call was made to check the key, per the safety contract.

findings.title: Sign-out clears the tokens but leaves the offline delivery cache with recipient PII on disk
findings.evidence: session.dart:68-73 removes the three auth prefs keys and the PIN entry. It does not touch courier_cache.db, which delivery_detail.dart:38 opens by name and which holds recipient, address, window_start, window_end, notes (delivery_detail.dart:41). Grep across the component finds no deleteDatabase and no other cleanup routine.
findings.impact: On a shared or reassigned fleet handset, the next driver's app retains the previous driver's recipient names, street addresses and delivery notes; DeliveryDetail renders any cached row by id from the local database without an API call. Also keeps third-party PII on the device indefinitely after the relationship ends, and inside the backup surface described in the allowBackup finding.
findings.recommendation: Delete or re-key the cache database in Session.clear (deleteDatabase, or SQLCipher keyed per session), so sign-out ends access to cached personal data as well as to the session.

triage.reason: A cleanup routine could live in the sign-out screen, which is not in this file set; nothing in the component performs it.
A second principal exists: the next driver to sign in on the same handset, and the recipients whose data is retained are third parties, not the account holder.
Recipient names and street addresses are personal data.

scope.established_by: clear() is the session teardown and enumerates four keys; the cache is not among them.
scope.narrowed_by: The cache lives in the app-private databases directory (a relative name at delivery_detail.dart:38, not external storage), so no other app reads it without root.

searched.for: any code that removes or re-keys the cache on sign-out
searched.found: nothing - courier_cache.db is opened at delivery_detail.dart:38 and never deleted

searched.for: whether the cached rows are per-driver scoped, which would bound the leak
searched.found: nothing - the query selects by delivery id alone, with no driver column in the projection

findings.what_would_settle_it: The sign-out screen, not included in this file set. If it deletes courier_cache.db, this is refuted; if it only calls Session.clear(), it is confirmed.
